newsitem.title: GERMANY: Berlin counts days until government moves from Bonn.
newsitem.headline: Berlin counts days until government moves from Bonn.

text.p: Berlin is counting the days until the government moves from Bonn, and Tuesday's groundbreaking ceremony for a new chancellery in the capital was an important milestone on the road towards the 1999 target date.

Momentum for the government's relocation eastwards has accelerated under the guidance of Construction Minister Klaus Toepfer, who in recent years mowed down diehard opponents of the move in Bonn with a deft and forceful hand.

By persuading most of the nine federal ministers set to move to Berlin along with the parliament to take over existing government-owned buildings rather than erect new ministries, Toepfer has saved time and money.

The cost of the move has been cut to under 20 billion marks ($12 billion) and the once-doubtful timetable of the move taking place between 1998 and 2000 put back on track. The 400-million mark chancellery is the final major building project.
Topefer has become a local hero in Berlin, the once-divided city that sometimes displays a surprising lack of confidence as it struggles to find a new identity in the post-Cold War era.
Berlin Mayor Eberhard Diepgen last year launched a "1,000-day countdown" for the government move.
That countdown was aimed at May 23, 1999 -- the day when an assembly representing both houses of parliament is due to gather in the renovated Reichstag to elect the next German president.
Many in government are endorsing May 1999 as a realistic date for the move.
But Rita Suessmuth, the president of the lower house, expects parliament to hold some sessions in Berlin as soon as the extensive renovation work on the Reichstag is completed.
"The parliament will start working in the Reichstag building at the start of 1999," Suessmuth said.

Optimism that the move will take place in early 1999 was further raised by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's recent decision to house the chancellery in the State Council Building -- the former seat of East Germany's collective presidency under Erich Honecker -- if the new building is not ready in time.

President Roman Herzog has already taken up residence in the robust city whose broad boulevards stand in stark contrast to the narrow avenues of Bonn, a small town of 300,000 on the banks of the Rhine river 600 km (360 miles) to the west.

Moving into existing buildings in Berlin will be the ministries for transport, economics, justice, finance as well as the federal press office. Part of the foreign ministry will be new and the interior ministry will rent a new office building.
Seven other ministries will stay in Bonn, which has fought hard to ensure it does not become a "ghost town" after the government leaves town.
Bonn has won the right to host the United Nations agencies for volunteers and climate convention as well as scientific institutes and non-governmental organisations.
About 18,500 federal workers are expected to pack their bags and white-collar shirts for the move to Berlin, Germany's largest city with 3.5 million people.
Tens of thousands of lobbyists, journalists and diplomats will be moving east at about the same time as the government.

A speculative bubble that sent real estate prices in Berlin shooting higher in the early 1990s after parliament voted narrowly in 1991 to move there has since burst. Prices for housing and office space have plunged as demand failed to keep up with the building boom.
The government is building 8,000 apartment units for government workers and is holding on to another 4,000 well-equipped apartments in leafy sections of town it rented to Allied soldiers.
The government rents about 200,000 square metres of office space in Bonn but will need only around 45,000 in Berlin because it already owns so many buildings in the capital. ($ = 1.640 German Marks)
